Our Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model has been designed to accurately forecast nonlinear, bursty time series with structural breaks. This model's key strength lies in its capacity to adapt to changing conditions throughout the series by allowing for time-varying parameters. In nonlinear dynamic environments with unknown break times, we've proven that TV-PARX can accurately identify the underlying structures and models. Furthermore, our model's modular formulation enables the incorporation of external influences that may impact the series. We've developed efficient algorithms to estimate TV-PARX model parameters and select important exogenous variables. This model's efficacy has been demonstrated through comprehensive simulations and real-world applications to a streaming financial dataset and a COVID-19 daily infection dataset.

Vertical aerosol optical depth's determination requires a reference point for calibration or a technique that relies on relative measurements. A novel method utilizing wide-field photometry's relative information was proposed and tested on three different events observed by the ATOM boomerang oven mass spectrometer and an all-sky camera system. Comparing the method to an established one based on absolute calibration showed similar accuracy when using the all-sky camera system but a significant advantage when using the ATOM boomerang oven mass spectrometer system. The study's findings suggest the new approach is a valuable tool for vertical aerosol optical depth's determination or other applications requiring precise optical depth information.

Numerous numerical methods exist for solving the partial differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations, and we assess two popular methods, the spectral and finite difference approaches, on a prototype biomolecular system, alanine dipeptide. Initial conditions that produce similar dynamics when solved analytically must be solved exactly for mild time steps, but may require more stringent time step constraints when solved numerically. We evaluate the accuracy and computational efficiency of these methods by comparing the solutions to the inhomogeneous free Schrödinger equation, considering various initial conditions, including oscillatory and complex configurations. The results show that the finite difference method exhibits linear convergence to the exact solution, whereas the spectral method has a more complex convergence behavior. Moreover, we examine the effect of the method's parameters on computational efficiency and accuracy, and provide theoretical estimates for the time step constraint in the finite difference approach. The study's findings highlight the importance of choosing suitable numerical methods to simulate biomolecular systems, and demonstrate the spectral method's superiority over the finite difference approach for solving the inhomogeneous free Schrödinger equation.

Users who are visually impaired often rely on image descriptions to navigate visually rich content.
Currently available descriptions may not accurately convey the intended meaning of images due to lack of specificity and ambiguity.
This issue persists even with the use of artificial intelligence generated descriptions.
To address this problem, we are proposing an enhanced framework for generating precise image descriptions.
This vision-and-language system utilizes a combination of attention mechanisms and generative models to accurately depict the visual elements in images.
In addition to describing images, this system can also predict the relationships between visible objects.
We have conducted extensive experiments using this system on various datasets, which have shown consistently improved performance over state-of-the-art methods.
These results demonstrate the potential of this approach to deliver detailed image descriptions that accurately reflect the true nature of images.

We provide a novel perspective on Euler-Arnold equations, demonstrating how they facilitate optimization within quantum field theory, specifically in connection with the stationary action principle and, more broadly, in relation to variational problems in general. A key role is played by Euler-Arnold's theorem ensuring an equivalence between distanced regularizing functionals and preorders defined on certain infinite-dimensional manifolds. A defining feature of Euler-Arnold equations is that they give rise to preorders, thereby enabling the resolution of optimization issues. A concise overview of key concepts is provided in the introduction, followed by a detailed examination of distance-regulating functionals and preorders, concluding with an exploration of the underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying underlying

The interaction between heavy quarks is a key area of study in QCD, with multiple theoretical approaches including perturbation theory, sum rules, and lattice QCD. Theoretical frameworks like NRQCD and HQET are used to study heavy quark interactions, with lattice QCD providing critical low-energy information. Recent lattice studies have confirmed the stability of charmed quark pairs and their decay characteristics. Similarly, lattice QCD has been successful in predicting properties of beauty quark pairs and their resulting particles, with recent studies focusing on near-threshold phenomena and the behavior of bottomonium states.

This research explores techniques for optimizing fair-throughput and total-throughput in wideband waveforming strategies, focusing on multi-user massive MIMO systems with partial channel knowledge. A novel algorithm is developed, incorporating an intelligent sweeping approach and an updated Genetric Algorithm to optimize wideband waveforming. The algorithm's efficiency is assessed by optimizing fair-throughput and total-throughput in comparison with existing methods, demonstrating significant improvements of up to three times in optimal throughput.

The determination of parton distribution functions (PDFs) is intricately linked with the use of the DGLAP evolution equations to calculate PDFs at varying scales. Typically, fit parameters are determined at a specific reference scale, and the DGLAP equations are used to compute PDFs at other scales. However, recent studies have revealed inconsistencies between employed PDF evolution codes, leading to disparities among various PDF fits. To address this issue, we conducted an in-depth examination of the DGLAP evolution implementation in the Durand-Raposo-Rocha (DDR) evolution package, which is a key component of many PDF fits. Upon identifying and fixing code abnormalities, we observed that the DDR implementation diverges from the conventional picture of PDF evolution. Specifically, we found that the DDR code produces distinct results compared to the built-in evolution capabilities in Mathematica and MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO. To reconcile these differences, we developed an alternative, mathematically rigorous DDR implementation utilizing the Mathematica package "Integrate." This revised version accurately captures the essence of the DDR evolution model, allowing for direct calculation of PDF derivatives without relying on numerical integration. Consequently, we observed that the revised implementation yields consistent outcomes with the reference codes. To ensure the integrity of future PDF fits, we recommend utilizing the revised DDR implementation or the built-in Mathematica routine "NIntegrate" to compute PDF evolution.

This research seeks to analyze and compare various active combustion models within a linearized framework, focusing on identifying the most suitable model for describing turbulent, reacting flows. A key enhancement to the framework, involving solving an additional equation for progress variable models, has been employed. Through this enhancement, models such as the EDLC and FSDLC can be analyzed within the linearized framework. Combustion models fall under the category of reaction rates in their general form, which can be linearized and analyzed. The analysis reveals that the FSDLC model exhibits the strongest coupling with the largest reaction rate, making it the best choice for describing turbulent, reacting flows.

We introduce a new constitutive relation within the framework of nonlocal gravity theory, which deviates from standard Einstein gravity only at extremely small scale distances. Using this relation, we derive a modified Poisson equation, and subsequently predict minor deviations in observable quantities such as the gravitational constant, the bond force, and the speed of gravitational waves.

Recent $pp$ collision data at 13 TeV, involving pseudorapidity distances less than one unit, exhibits only slight increases in strange particle production relative to non-strange particles. However, as the separation between particles exceeds one unit of pseudorapidity, the data shows a significant enhancement in strange particle production, displaying a pattern similar to that observed in heavy-ion collisions.

The connection between neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) and millisecond pulsars remains unclear due to limited information. A previous study identified possible locations of 74 millisecond pulsars within 5 kiloparsecs of the Sun. However, only a small fraction of these pulsars have been found near known LMXB populations. To better understand this relationship, we examined the population parameters of LMXBs and millisecond pulsars using the REAST code. Initially, we assumed both populations evolved from similar initial conditions. Despite this assumption, we found significant differences between their birth and current locations. The discrepancy arose because many LMXBs have undergone significant supernova kicks during their formation. By accounting for these kicks, we mapped the pre-explosion environments of LMXBs, which sometimes extended far from their current locations. This more accurate mapping showed that the overall structure of the LMXB population remained consistent, even after considering various model inputs. Ultimately, we identified a correlation between the population densities of LMXBs and millisecond pulsars across the Galactic center region. This connection suggests that both populations might share a common formation site, with many LMXBs transforming into millisecond pulsars over time.

This research paper investigates techniques for guaranteeing the planarity of bipartite graphs through vertex splitting and the resulting drawability in a 2-dimensional space. A novel algorithm is developed to accomplish this task in O(e^2 log e) time, where e represents the edge count of the graph. Additionally, the paper explores the applications of vertex splitting in ensuring the drawability of bipartite graphs under specific conditions, as well as creating linear representations of the big and small sets through the algorithm.

Recent attacks such as Flush+Reload have gained popularity for exploiting side-channel information, specifically the time granularity of modern operating systems. In a typical Flush+Reload attack, the attacker measures the time between flushing cache lines and accessing their memory location. Recent studies have optimized this protocol by introducing various techniques, including HyperDegrade. This study extends the HyperDegrade technique to create a more efficient Flush+Reload attack, which requires less time and fewer measurement traces than previous methods. This enhanced protocol, which we call FGR, offers a time granularity of 50 nanoseconds with only 10 measurement traces. In contrast, the HyperDegrade technique only offers a time granularity of 1 millisecond with 1000 measurement traces. This research further explores the FGR protocol by designing multiple variants, each offering a different time granularity, and analyzing the protocol's vulnerability to various interference sources, including page faults and disk I/O operations.
Our study introduces the concept of stretching moves called diagonal moves for basic knotted structures, specifically for the purposes of enhancement and analysis.

In collaborative systems where tasks are shared among agents, predicting the performance of each agent can be complicated, and decision-making about task allocation might be more practical. We propose an unsupervised learning method called Representative-Based Off-Policy Evaluation to address this challenge. It utilizes a small sample of observed task allocations, comparing the performance of agents under different scenarios, allowing for the estimation of the true reward for any given allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in a realistic simulation of a smart energy management system, showing significant improvements over off-policy estimation methods.

We provide a definition for a key concept, highlighting its characteristics and and demonstrating how it relates to other important ideas in geometry. This concept is particularly notable in the context of buildings and joins a list of already established principles, including those related to regular group actions and a specific type of subgroup called diagonal groups. A notable outcome from this definition is a proof that buildings with structures influenced by these groups exhibit a form of geometry known as Cartesian decomposition.

Quantifying gravitational wave strains near the limit of sensitivity requires accurate measurement of faint signals between optical carrier and Sagnac interferometer output light. Traditional differential interferometry relies on signal subtraction which is prone to errors. A novel technique, called sloshing-Sagnac interferometry, uses the carrier light to measure the signal light's phase directly, offering a precise method for extracting weak optical signals. This method's sensitivity is evaluated for a simple model and a full parameter estimation study on a binary black hole merger signal. Compared to standard Sagnac interferometry, sloshing-Sagnac provides an order of magnitude improvement in strain sensitivity (10^-23 strain accuracy within 100 seconds of data integration) and reduces systematic errors associated with signal subtraction.

To address performance degradation in wideband XL-MIMO systems during random access, we propose a new protocol called NOVR-XL RA. This protocol builds upon the existing NOVR framework and incorporates an additional step to handle massive codebook search. The proposed NOVR-XL RA utilizes a compressive sensing based approach to reduce the codebook size while maintaining snapshot quality. As a result, NOVR-XL RA outperforms the state-of-the-art TUR-based approach, specifically in scenarios with a large number of antennas and wideband transmissions. Theoretical performance analysis indicates that the NOVR-XL RA achieves near-optimal performance with a significant reduction in codeword search complexity.

Neural language models have been highly effective in predicting the next word in a sequence, but they require large amounts of computational data and often struggle with unfamiliar topics. On the other hand, $N$-gram models are simple, require less data, and work well with new information but predict only a single word at a time. Here, we propose a hybrid approach called NeuralGram, which leverages the strengths of both models by using the neural model to generate multiple words and then applying an $N$-gram model to refine the output. In experiments on English-French machine translation, a commonly used dataset showed significant improvements over conventional methods, achieving state-of-the-art results with minimal tuning required. Additionally, NeuralGram performed well in an automatic summarization experiment using a large English corpus, outperforming both recurrent and transformer-based neural models.

The reliability of optical character recognition in vote tabulation relies heavily on precise font recognition. However, font variations and inconsistencies can lead to recognition errors, necessitating the use of spell checkers to correct these mistakes. We've developed an advanced spell checker, called Levenshtein Rationalized Spell Checker (LRSC), which builds on the basic spell checking function to enhance accuracy. In a comprehensive evaluation involving 24 fonts and multiple scenarios, LRSC consistently outperformed the standard spell checker, with improvement rates ranging from 20% to 90% for single-character changes and 40% to 99.9% for overall correction rates. These results demonstrate LRSC's capability to effectively mitigate font-related recognition errors, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of optical character recognition in vote tabulation systems.

This study utilizes a global climate model to simulate an Earth-like atmosphere, focusing on a specific scenario with low solar activity. Under these conditions, we observed the development of baroclinic storms in the model, resembling the Great Dark Spot on Mars. By analyzing the temperature and wind patterns, we found similarities between the Martian baroclinic storms and the simulated Earth-like atmosphere, including the presence of an equatorial jet and subtropical highs. Additionally, we noted the formation of low-pressure systems near the storm edges and the role of the Hadley and Ferrel circulation cells in maintaining these patterns.

Our study develops complex representations of the gamma and psi functions using complex paths, specifically Hankel paths, integrated in the z-plane between the positive reals and the negative reals. We first prove that this Hankel path represents the gamma function, then derive the psi function as its derivative. The resulting representation for the psi function is in a form that showcases its relation to the gamma function.

Quantum systems' non-equilibrium behavior and correlations are challenging to predict with traditional methods, but a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme may offer a more efficient way to simulate these phenomena. This study investigates how a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme, in combination with a simplified single-particle density matrix approach, enhances non-equilibrium quantum correlations compared to using traditional methods. Using a simple model, we validated the scheme's accuracy by reproducing established results for the steady-state current-phase relationship and the nanoscale electric field's influence on polymer chain configurations. Furthermore, we explored the scheme's capability in simulating the behavior of larger polyatomic molecules, demonstrating its potential for predicting correlated quantum states and evaluating the scheme's numerical costs.

Our proposed method, called Knowledge Refining Hard Excitation (KRHE), focuses on the hard excitation step in the hard example mining process for distribution-aware knowledge distillation.  Initially, a lightweight student network learns from a pre-trained deep teacher network in a hard-excitation manner, generating hard features that are then refined using an additional network.  By doing so, KRHE produces more accurate knowledge and reduces inter-class feature overlap, leading to better performance compared to existing methods.  In addition, KRHE introduces a new regularisation technique called feature dispersion, which enhances the distinctness of features further.  Experiments on three datasets - CIFAR100, ImageNet, and Flowers92 - demonstrate that KRHE achieves the highest accuracy compared to other methods, showing its effectiveness in facilitating hard-exitation based knowledge distillation.

We introduce Bucket Elimination with Sorting (BES), an optimized algorithm for inference and optimization tasks in graphical models, specifically designed to build upon Bucket Elimination (BE) and benefit from the advantages of Minimum Equivalent Graph reduction. By integrating BE with the technique of sorting nodes based on their connectivity, we enhance the efficiency of BES compared to its precursor, without incurring additional computational costs. Through exhaustive testing on various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that BES consistently outperforms BE, as well as other established methods like CPG and MFG, in terms of time consumption and memory utilization.

The paper under review presents a novel method for determining parts of the Hilbert-Poincaré series of centralizer algebras, specifically for the sl2 Lie algebra, particularly when acting on the tensor product of representations.

This paper introduces an exact statistical testing procedure known as the paired-permutation test, which assesses whether there's a significant dependency between paired data sequences. This test can be applied to both fixed and infinite numbers of data pairs, and it comes with time-consuming but practical computational methods. However, when the size of the data is substantial, these methods may not be efficient. In contrast, a simple alternative using a Monte Carlo approximation exists but with an elevated risk of producing inaccurate results. 

To resolve this efficiency issue, we've developed an new exact algorithm which takes a paired-permutation test as input and outputs the test result, capable of handling vast data sets with minimal computational expense. This new algorithm proves to have significantly better computational times than the practical methods mentioned earlier when we tested it on real-life massive data sets from the scientific community, which takes several orders of magnitude longer to compute than other feasible cases. 

In the case of fixed data sizes, this new algorithm achieves the same precision as the practical methods; in the case of infinite data sizes, it yields the true underlying statistics through the asymptotic property of the paired-permutation test.

Recent data on $v_2(\pt)$ and $\Delta v_3/\Delta S_3$ from STAR and ALICE exhibits a surprising similarity between elliptical flow and triangular flow's transverse momentum dependence for identified particles. Understanding the connection between these two flows is crucial for reconstructing initial state geometry. Given that elliptical and triangular shapes are fundamental components in geometry, their similar $\pt$ dependance suggests their ratio might reflect the true shape ratio $3\pi/4$ and thus the initial conditions.

The structure of the underlying domain is continuously updated when targets move and sensors have limited fields of view. To efficiently manage this, we've developed a method that uses a joint graph model, incorporating both sensor information and target movements. This model enables us to quickly identify newly appearing targets and reconfigure the graph seamlessly. By doing so, we can maintain a precise map of the environment without excessive computation, even in large spaces with limited sensor vision.

The potential reward of taking a shot on goal compared to maintaining possession, as well as the decision to pass instead of shoot in soccer, can be influenced by the actions that occur before the scenario. A key factor in this decision-making process is the location of the ball following an action like committing a foul or the ball going out of bounds. This study examines the relative value of taking a shot on goal versus maintaining possession in these situations, utilizing an expected goal model. It finds that regaining possession is more valuable when the opponent scores or a foul is committed, but less so in cases of offside calls or the ball going out of bounds.

The integration of artificial intelligence for automating laboratory experiments has shown significant potential in response to increased telework demands. As researchers remotely access and control experiments, the need for automated setups has grown, presenting opportunities for AI to enhance the process. Currently, various options exist for automating experiments using AI, including the employment of neural networks to optimize parameters and automate data analysis. Moreover, there are possibilities for incorporating domain knowledge into automated workflows, enabling the creation of tailored, AI-driven laboratory experiments. As a result, we are seeing a convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, and the internet of things in laboratories, paving the way for a future "laboratory 4.0" where AI and humans collaborate to conduct experiments.

We investigate the stability of solitary waves in a system where a mass $m$ is connected to an anharmonic oscillator. Previously, it has been found that certain shapes of solitary waves could emerge in this system. Here, we determine the conditions under which solitary wave stability is ensured, and we identify the specific characteristics of these waves. We also examine the stability of these solitary waves in a system where the anharmonic oscillator is replaced by a harmonic oscillator, and we derive the limits beyond which the solitary wave transitions back to a pulse-like state.

The paper undertakes an in-depth examination of parameters that affect the optimization of search strategies for neutral long-lived particles (NLLPs) at colliders, with a focus on the decay length threshold. A threshold that is too low may detect the particle but not its properties, whereas one that is too high might miss the signal entirely. To address this challenge, we define a signal region with an intermediate decay length threshold. This region enables the separation of the NLLP from other decay modes, allowing for the calculation of significant event yields and sensitivity measures. Using the framework, we investigate how the decay length threshold impacts the performance of search strategies for both prompt and displaced scenarios. The results reveal that an optimal threshold enhances detection potential, with significant gains observed for certain scenarios. Furthermore, we observe a direct correlation between the decay length threshold and the minimum particle production cross-section that can be detected.

A challenge in analyzing language's steady evolution is pinpointing exactly how subtle changes in context influence word meanings. Typically, we assess the impact of contextual variance on semantic shift identification. However, recent advances in method development have left this issue unexplored. In a breakthrough study, researchers claimed that contextual variance doesn't significantly affect how we define and identify semantic shifts. To resolve this dispute, we designed an exhaustive evaluation examining the effect of contextual variance on identifying semantic shifts. Our results reveal that contextual variance indeed affects the identification of semantic shifts. We found that medium-sized changes in contextual variance lead to a significant increase in identifying semantic shifts, and this optimal range is particularly valuable when analyzing shifts in animal names.

Recent observations of galactic bulges suggest that dark matter may not be present in certain regions. A recent study has re-examined the assumption that ultra-light bosonic dark matter particles behave as waves in certain environments. If these particles form the dark matter in galactic bulges, they would be in a state of quantum macroscopic superposition, making their particle properties extremely light, even approaching the quantum limit. However, recent experimental limits on the properties of these particles do not support such an idea. As a result, it is not possible to explain the composition of dark matter in bulges using these theoretical models. Alternatively, if the models are applicable in specific situations, the observations could imply the presence of a'repulsive core' in the boson fossil field theory, or the models might be inconsistent with certain consistency relations.

Quantum systems subjected to continuous driving are investigated here, focusing on the role of coherent state inputs. A general framework is established, utilizing the input-output picture, to analyze driven quantum systems in arbitrary environments. The framework enables the assessment of system-reservoir coupling strengths, even when the driving source is strongly coupled to the system. Furthermore, the framework allows determining the effective reservoir influence, allowing for the identification of limits on system stability and the onset of non-equilibrium behavior.

We have developed a quantum relational Hoare logic that enables the specification of conditional relationships between programs' inputs and outputs. This logic extends the traditional relational specification to accommodate probabilistic outcomes resulting from quantum programs. A key feature of this logic is the introduction of both relational and distance-based predicates to describe the relationship between inputs and outputs. We have defined validational theorems for both relational and distance-based predicates, demonstrating the logic's capability to quantify the connection between inputs and outputs through relational and differential metrics.

This research presents an enhancement to an existing method for accurately determining magnetic fields within photospheric vector magnetic field maps. The improved technique explicitly considers the filled area of magnetic features, which contributor significantly to the method's accuracy issues. By incorporating fill fraction information into calculations, more precise values for magnetic field strengths can be achieved, especially in densely packed areas. Furthermore, this modification enables the determination of magnetic flux densities even in partially filled pixels, expanding the method's utility.

For a Coxeter group with a distinguished generating set, we develop a symbolic computation tool that explores the geometry of reduced words, specifically within a given wedge of spheres. This tool is then employed to investigate how the size of the generating set affects various properties of words, including the number of spheres in a wedge, counting representatives of each conjugacy class, and determining the depth of words.
This research paper verifies the statement claiming that all Bertrand curves in the Euclidean plane have a specific geometric definition.

This paper investigates the potential for specific, under-represented loss functions in neural network development, specifically the Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence loss, which has been largely bypassed in favour of MSE loss in regression tasks. To address this, the paper proposes three models: a basic model using MSE loss, a shallow model that requires KL loss to achieve comparable performance, and a deep model where KL loss is necessary for improving performance beyond the basic model. Evaluating these models using objective loss evaluation (OLE) and the representative loss (ReL) framework, reveals impressive results for the shallow and deep models demonstrating the effectiveness of KL loss.

Neural models have been successfully applied to natural language reasoning tasks, exhibiting high accuracy with little understanding of the underlying structural reasons. This study investigates the underlying factors contributing to the effectiveness of neural models when trained on if-then relation types, which are categorized hierarchically as follows: Cause-Condition, Possessive, Reciprocal, Inclusive, Distributive, and Purposive-Accomplishable. Contrary to previous research, research highlights that specific relation types do not necessitate the integration of external knowledge graphs. Instead, the study demonstrates that the majority of if-then relation types can be identified based solely on semantic features. Furthermore, the research shows that neural models benefit substantially from training on the hierarchical structure of relation types, exhibiting accuracy of 90.4% compared to 75.3% when using a flat classification approach.

Our proposed method makes enhanced predictions of novel-view videos by incorporating a novel dual representation into the conventional neural operator. The dual representation consists of an inverse operator and a complementary operator, which are derived from the fundamental principle of linear system theory. Unlike existing methods that rely on additional supervision or specific data, the derived dual representation requires no additional information. This is because the dual representation is inherently included in the linear system model. Our method demonstrates consistent improvements in novel-view video prediction across various datasets, according to our experimental results.

We provide exact formulas to determine the minimum number of distinguishing landmarks in a given graph based on a truncated distance, as well as in its original form, by establishing a direct connection to the minimum number of landmarks required in the graph's substructure derived from its connectivity components.

Our proposed method tackles beat detection accuracy degradation when using wearable GPS for heart rate estimation, particularly in noisy settings. This method combines a regularizer and a convolutional neural network to enhance the quality of noisy GPS data, reducing interference from excessive movement. This interference commonly causes false interpretations of cardiac signals, particularly between adjacent beats, making it challenging to identify patterns and anomalies. By minimizing regularized loss functions, we can reduce noise-induced artefacts and improve the detection of cardiac abnormalities.

We have discovered several instances of far-reaching ionized winds or gas reservoirs surrounding starburst galaxies using deep optical spectroscopy from the MUSE instrument on the VLT. These discoveries were made during a 80-hour survey of 52 extreme starburst galaxies selected from the CDF-S and EGS fields. Many of these winds exhibit irregular shapes and some have broken links to their host galaxies. One galaxy, CGF4, was found to have a massive, detached gas reservoir approximately 50 kiloparsecs from its host. The line ratios within these winds or reservoirs often indicate the presence of circumgalactic or wind gas with low density, contradicting the high electron densities found within the galaxy's central region. However, some line ratios from specific locations showed signs of both low and high electron densities, indicating variable conditions within both the winds and reservoirs.
We establish explicit, recursive formulas to calculate the probability distribution of a second-class particle's velocity in ASEP (Artificial Spin Ice) at any given time.

Epidemiological studies often employ differential equations to model disease dynamics and understand the impact of interventions. A key aspect of these studies is determining the underlying contact rates between population groups, which serves a vital function in shaping disease behavior and understanding the effects of interventions. In many cases, researchers aim to estimate contact rates from available data, which may involve mortuary records, infected individual data, and testing information. A critical condition ensuring the uniqueness of the model's solution is that the contact rate between infected and healthy individuals must be greater than the contact rate between healthy individuals, which holds true in many scenarios, including the recent COVID-19 pandemic. However, researchers have recently raised concerns about the biological plausibility of this differential model, particularly in the context of homogeneous mixing populations, following the outbreak of the SARS-CoV2 pandemic, which led to widespread lockdowns and other control measures. In such instances, the condition mentioned above may not be met, which raises a significant methodological issue. To address this challenge, we propose a modified differential model that accounts for available vaccinations, which have become a crucial tool in combating the pandemic. The proposed model extends the existing framework and ensures that its solution is unique, even in scenarios where further lockdown measures or other contact-reducing interventions are implemented.

Our research examined the relationship between galaxy mass and NUV-r color through observations of 600,000 galaxies collected by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Contrary to expectations, we discovered that low-mass galaxies exhibit similar NUV-r colors. However, once we removed galaxies with extremely blue colors, we found a positive correlation between mass and NUV-r color for galaxies above a threshold of 10^9.5 M solar masses. Moreover, this correlation aligns with the star formation history predicted by models of galaxy evolution, with no additional information required beyond mass.

One potential approach to accomplish cross-language sentiment classification involves using multilingual pre-trained models and modifying their output layers to classify sentiments. This technique can be particularly effective with large datasets. In situations where smaller datasets are available, an alternative method is to fine-tune the model's output layer and generate the necessary training data through machine translation.

We undertook a performance analysis of the KIC 9267654 star, which exhibits an unusual rotation profile with multiple components. Initially, we ruled out any convolution effects resulting from instrumentation or data processing. Furthermore, we excluded the possibility of the profile's second component representing a shear velocity curve, due to insufficient separation between the speeds of the two components. Additionally, we dismissed the idea that the feature could be attributed to non-localized bulk motion within the star, as there was insufficient energy present. We also considered and dismissed possible causes including gravity modes, seismic standing waves, and the presence of a companion star. Ultimately, we found that a model featuring a localized, non-rigid interior region provided the most plausible explanation for the observed feature. This model involves a significant chemical disparity between the core and the rest of the star, which could potentially arise in extremely massive stars or those with enhanced helium flash behavior. On the other hand, an alternative explanation involving a tidal inertial wave generated by a close-by companion star also showed promise, particularly in cases where the star's mass is substantially elevated.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms.
This research develops MetaFEND, a deep learning-based system to help
detect false information. Unlike similar systems, MetaFEND utilizes
multiple categories of Facebook posts to detect false information.
To train and evaluate MetaFEND, researchers created a large dataset
consisting of true and false information on three platforms: Facebook,
Instagram, and Twitter. The results show that MetaFEND outperforms
existing systems in detecting false information, with the highest
accuracy achieved at 97.5% on the Twitter dataset.

Designing Golay complementary arrays, which are crucial for multiplexing and simultaneous localization in wireless sensor networks, presents a challenge, especially when considering four-dimensional coordinates. Despite the existing methods for finding Golay complementary arrays in binary and ternary spaces, creating pairs of such arrays in quadruple-dimensional spaces remains uncertain. To address this uncertainty, we develop new construction approaches for quaternary Golay complementary array pairs on an $n\times n$ grid. Moreover, we outline the necessary conditions that must be satisfied for such a construction to be feasible. Reaching this verdict, we determine the specific parameters that must be met: $n\leq 47$ and $4n\leq 947$.

Deep learning algorithms have become increasingly vital for accurate region-of-interest (ROI) segmentation in medical imaging. This work investigates the underlying factors that contribute to the effective segmentation of ROIs using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and a widely used architecture, U-Net. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and computational experiments, we demonstrate that nearly perfect segmentation results can be achieved with a simplified model that consists of only a few CNN layers. This simplified model reveals the key role that CNNs play in boosting segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, we identify the critical aspect of spatial resolution in image scanning, which significantly affects segmentation outcomes. We also introduce an innovative method to decompose CNN output gradients, enabling a deeper understanding of the segmentation process and facilitating the development of optimized imaging protocols.

This paper introduces a unified framework for both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction, resolving the existing gap between supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. The proposed method, called the Iterative Discriminative Common Space Learning (IDCSL) approach, generates a between-class discriminative common space without requiring labeled data. By iteratively refining this space, we can extract informative features even in completely unsupervised scenarios. Furthermore, the framework allows for the incorporation of supervised information when labeled data is available, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of image classification problems.

Our investigation introduces a new concept, Knowledge Infusion Multilingual Transformers (KIMT), where multilingual transformer models are pre-trained on a vast amount of knowledge-infused triples derived from knowledge graphs and their associated text. We present two KIMT models, one based on BERT and another on RoBERTa, and evaluate their performance in question-answering tasks compared to traditional pre-training methods. Results show that B-KIMT outperforms BART-large by 31.2% on WIKI-QM and that R-KIMT surpasses RuBert-large by 24.3% on ZhiYe-QA. Additionally, we observe that B-KIMT performs better than BART-large on 10 out of 12 datasets and that R-KIMT outperforms RuBert-large on 11 out of 12 datasets.

We undertook a comprehensive examination of how non-linear Yang-Mills charges impact the shadow radius and thermal profile of black holes. In a framework with non-linear electrodynamics, we evaluated the effects of charge distribution on both the shadow radius and the thermal profile through their relationships with the electromagnetic field. A key discovery was that the shadow radius of the black hole horizon shows no dependence on the non-linear Yang-Mills charge. However, we found that the thermal profile is influenced by the charge, leading to an enhanced thermal zone outside the event horizon. Additionally, we observed that the maximum temperature at the black hole's surface remains unaffected by the non-linear Yang-Mills charge. A notable finding was that the near-horizon thermal profile mirrors the pattern of charge distribution, demonstrating a clear boundary between two distinct thermal zones for a split charge configuration. We further verified that our findings align with those concerning the linear Yang-Mills charge, under the condition that the charge is uniformly distributed. A notable outcome was that the Fermi acceleration principle explains the influence of charge distribution on the thermal profile. We concluded that both linear and non-linear Yang-Mills charges have a similar impact on the thermal profile of black holes, with the former representing a special case of the latter.

We undertook a comprehensive analysis of how non-classical effects, specifically entanglement and squeezed states, emerge in the context of optical tomography. Initially, we established a connection between entanglement and the Wigner function's non-positive partial transpose attribute. Subsequently, we mapped this attribute to the optical tomogram, revealing the precise conditions under which non-classicality manifests through distinct shapes. In the case of entangled states, this results in an "hourglass" shape. Moreover, we observed that the tomographic region defining non-classicality might not always coincide with the positive density matrix regime, especially when considering entanglement first. Finally, we explored the relationship between entanglement, squeezed states and the Wigner function's negative domain.

The underlying structure of particles was examined by measuring the branching fractions of specific decay modes. Using 1.7 billion pairs of an electron and its opposite particle, the branching fraction of the phi particle decaying into two mesons called K+S was measured at a 6.5 sigma level of certainty and compared to the branching fraction of the phi particle decaying into two K mesons. Additionally, the branching fraction of the phi particle decaying into two K+ mesons, each decaying into muon and anti-muon, was measured at a 3.5 sigma level of certainty.

We provide new proofs for two established results in module theory. Firstly, we prove that submodules of multiplicity-free modules have a lattice structure that mirrors the lattice structure of the parent module. Secondly, we demonstrate that submodules of multiplicity-free modules only appear as composition factors within the lattice of submodules of the given module.

This research explores the geometric characteristics of biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space, particularly focusing on conditions that result in these surfaces being minimal. We conduct an in-depth examination of how recurrent directions influence these conditions, as well as the impact of recurrent directions on the second fundamental form of these hypersurfaces. Additionally, we investigate the consequences of these hypersurfaces being totally geodesic, and the outcomes when these surfaces are subject to harmonic and biharmonic operator constraints.

We provide a definition for p/q-recognisable subsets of (N_p/q)d in the form of identifying patterns within patterns. More specifically, we start with the initial structure of (N_p/q)d and then apply a sequence of substitutions, ultimately arriving at a form where we can easily define rational recognisability.

The Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks represent two distinct methods for parametrizing decay rate variations with respect to environmental changes. While both frameworks originate from effective field theory, they employ different approaches to describe how decay rates respond to modification. The Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert framework focuses on relativistic particle physics, utilizing the Schrödinger equation to analyze decay rate variations. In contrast, the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed framework is based on effective field theory, employing a derivative expansion to describe how decay rates adapt to changes in environmental conditions.

This study examines the theoretical underpinnings of a proposed method for calculating the Lyapunov exponent from time-series data. A rigorous mathematical derivation is provided to demonstrate that the exponent's finite value is a hallmark of stability within a dynamical system. The study's findings are then applied to validate the performance of the characterizing method.

This research expands upon the concept of an angle function, initially developed in a straightforward manner for Euclidean space, and then generalized for hyperbolic spaces in two dimensions. We enhance this definition to suit domains within certain geometric spaces, including the hyperbolic plane, and show that it mirrors the characteristics of an angle in those areas. Additionally, we demonstrate that this definition is equivalent to the true angle measure in those spaces.

Our study introduces the TPC (Transposed Point Cloud) framework, aimed at enhancing neural network models for point cloud processing, by incorporating a transposed point cloud component that mimics twisting transformations. This move enables models to focus on distinguishing between uniquely aligned points, rather than relying on geometric properties, thereby enhancing their robustness against twisting transformations. As an initial exploration, we developed a basic TPC block and demonstrated its effectiveness. Furthermore, we expanded the concept to a transposed point cloud residual block and then a transposed point cloud convolutional block, each with its respective theoretical analysis.

The integration of error detection and correction tools into programming environments can enhance the learning process for programmers, especially beginners.  This paper investigates the effectiveness of an automated testing environment that provides real-time feedback on mistakes made while coding.  Initially, the environment is described, focusing on its ability to identify common errors and offer fixing suggestions.  Then, an experimental design is outlined, where 60 intermediate-level programmers are divided into two groups: an experimental group using the automated environment and a control group using traditional error identification methods.  Both groups complete the same set of programming tasks under time constraints.  The results show that individuals using the automated environment exhibit better performance, experience less frustration, and demonstrate improved problem-solving strategies compared to those using traditional error identification methods.  Furthermore, the paper examines the types of errors that cause the greatest difficulty for programmers and discusses implications for teaching programming courses.  The findings suggest that such an environment can lead to more effective learning and reduced error rates when coding.
The $K$-Artin-Scheier cocycle for a given extension of $p$-divisible groups is defined as the $p$-reduction of the crystalline extension.

This study develops a novel method for utilizing a genetic algorithm to optimize sensor placement within composites that sense damage through changes in electrical resistance. Unlike visual damage, impacts from drops can cause subtle resin fractures with minimal external visibility, making detection more challenging. To address this, a laboratory experiment was designed where a unidirectional carbon composite undergos low-energy drops and the NixL relationship is harnessed to localize damage through electrical resistance variations. By applying the genetic algorithm to a finite element model of the composite, the results show a significant enhancement in identifying fracture locations with only a few strategically placed sensors. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the genetic algorithm can be combined with machine learning models to enhance damage detection accuracy by utilizing a larger sensor network.

We prove the integral identities resulting in the coefficients of the three-dimensional Euler-Poisson equation's power series expansion through the use of geometric vector techniques and the Dirac notation.
For actions of right-angled Artin groups on trees, a notable property is one where a separating subgraph's closure under edge connection and group action doesn't cover the entire tree.

This research paper discusses the development of two novel convergence speed enhancement techniques for the Nested Neumann (NN) algorithm, which is used to solve structured low-rank matrix singular value problems. The paper's primary contribution lies in proving that these techniques significantly accelerate the algorithm's convergence rate without compromising its established convergence properties.

We provide an in-depth examination of a contextual linear bandit problem where we propose two new algorithms that incorporate knowledge of the context distribution. This additional information differentiates our approach from a previously established bound. In situations where the context distribution is known, we demonstrate that the optimal policy can be precisely determined with a low communication cost of at most three bits.

A theoretical model has been developed to examine the influence of dust growth on cooling rates within the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. This region, characterized by low temperatures and peace-time particle collisions, is prone to dust accumulation. As particles combine through collisions, they may enter a sticky dust regime where settling occurs. To accurately assess the impact of this regime on cooling rates, a new theoretical approach was employed, focusing on the role of particles in absorbing and transporting heat. In this model, dust particles behave as an continuum medium, allowing for heat diffusion and absorption through radiation. Using this framework, we calculated the cooling rate in a given reference scenario. The results showed an enhancement in cooling rates when particles transition from the free-falling regime to the sticky dust regime. Furthermore, by treating dust as a continuum, we observed an increase in cooling rate in a given reference scenario.

On a gradient-shrinking Ricci soliton that is minimally parabolic, we establish a sharp bound of $C(r)\cdot e^{o(t)}$ for harmonic functions as their relation to growth conditions is clarified.  This bound's derivation relies on a novel approach that contrasts the standard method using maximum principles.  In this soliton geometry, we demonstrate that harmonic functions coincide with those of linear growth.  This discovery signifies that their dimension can be precisely determined at a specific distance $t$ from the metric's transformation center.  This discovery has significant implications, especially in the context of the Chen-Kennedy-Ruille show's harmonic core hypothesis.  This hypothesis is crucial for identifying the harmonic core in the following manner: outside a certain bounded region, a harmonic function behaves linearly.  This discovery is also significant for understanding the relationship between harmonic functions and the growth conditions they satisfy, which differ significantly from those met by Stein's theory in analytic hypersurface geometry.

Recent research on neural network security has experienced a surge in interest in dynamic backdoor attacks. These attacks aim to modify how a model behaves in response to trigger-based input manipulation. Although static backdoor attacks have shown potential, especially in image classification, dynamic attacks are more difficult to implement and have limited applicability. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new concept called trigger-aware embedding and tackles dynamic backdoor attacks in various classification tasks. In a comprehensive study, we devise three dynamic backdoor attack strategies that can be applied across multiple tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of these methods on popular deep learning models.

In models where data is distributed and learning from it is collaborative, consistency between local models often needs to be ensured before updating them. A common method for achieving this consistency is through the random walk approach on a graph, whose nodes represent data points and edges represent similarity between them. However, this method is computationally expensive and hard to scale, particularly when dealing with large datasets. To address this challenge, we're introducing a random walk model based on a consensus message, which reduces communication needs by processing data through a random walk on a graph. This random walk can be seen as a sequence of Metropolis-Hastings samplings, with each sampling depending on the previous one. To speed up the process and decrease communication costs, we derive an unbiased estimate of the desired statistic by using a Markov chain theorem. This results in an iterative algorithm that can be optimized using existing tools, in this case, the stochastic gradient. To evaluate the algorithm's accuracy, we derive a concentration inequality for the random walk-based sample average.

This research seeks to explore the effectiveness of interpolation-based mixing as a regularization technique in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Unlike other methods that utilize label noise resistance, this approach utilizes the underlying mechanism of interpolation, which produces a mixture of clean and noisy labels. By generating this blend, regularization is achieved and training can be carried out in a supervised setting. Experiments on publicly available datasets, specifically SSFA and SSBrain, demonstrate that this technique, when combined with a prominent segmentation model, delivers performance comparable to state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, and in some cases, outperforms them.

Quantum systems' nonlocal properties such as steering and entanglement have been extensively explored. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of single-particle entanglement's contribution to nonlocal effects and steering in multi-partite systems. Utilizing the entanglement monotony of concurrence, we demonstrated that single-particle entanglement is directly responsible for genuine steering. Moreover, we established a clear correlation between single-particle entanglement and genuine nonlocal effects, confirming that true nonlocality originates from the particle-level. This research provides a new perspective on the relationship between entanglement, steering, and nonlocality, offering a framework for identifying the source of nonlocality within complex systems.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and Internet-connected vehicles has created substantial security and privacy concerns. To address these issues, we are proposing a Blockchain-based system that utilizes a consortium architecture and Smart Contracts to ensure veracity in Information Systems for Vehicles. This proposed system features a five-layer structure consisting of Perception Layer, Data Layer, Intelligence Layer, Application Layer, and Extension Layer. To further enhance security and privacy, we are also introducing a Homomorphic Encryption protocol based on the Beaver Triple technique. The goal of this protocol is to encrypt and process vehicle data in a manner that is compatible with AI algorithms. We have conducted extensive security and privacy analyses to verify the effectiveness of our proposed method. The results demonstrate that our approach can resist various security threats and attacks.
To address hardware acceleration limitations, a proposed FDHT-LSTM circuit is being presented, which outperforms a benchmark tensor-decomposed approach in all evaluated scenarios.

Recent developments have led to a deeper understanding of the structure of Galois groups within function fields. As a result, researchers may be closer to answering the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture's primary question. Nonetheless, the current state of knowledge falls short of providing a direct proof. Nevertheless, a significant outcome is the confirmation that there exist power-free, irreducible polynomials with respect to the following specification: their set of prime factors does not include 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and 17. Moreover, for any given positive integer $n$, there exists a power-free, irreducible polynomial whose set of prime factors fully encompasses the numbers 2 through $n$.

This work examines the methods employed to prove blow-up in solutions of the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a boundary, and reveals that standard approaches yield only minimal information concerning the dynamics of solutions near the boundary. A key finding is that boundary-specific information cannot be obtained through these methods, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of blow-up phenomena, particularly in the case of the exterior dimension one Schrödinger equation with a rigid boundary.

This article examines the connection between commutative algebras over fields of characteristic zero and those over fields of positive characteristic. We establish an equivalence between certain properties in characteristic zero and their counterparts in positive characteristic through the use of the characteristic function.

Utilities represent the level of desirability or value attached to specific outcomes or hypotheses in various scientific disciplines. A key challenge in hypothesis testing lies in making data-driven decisions based on utility functions, as it involves choosing the hypothesis that leads to the most desirable outcome. This rationale underlies the proposal to use utility functions in selecting hypotheses, which can be viewed as an input parameter. This vision is particularly relevant for adaptive decision-making processes, where the available data may not suffice to confirm or reject a hypothesis but can still be employed to determine which one yields the best outcome.

Discourse markers play a significant role in communicating relationships between sentences. Despite their importance, there's a lack of multi-language datasets that focus on discourse markers and their associated relations. To address this gap, we present DiscSense, the first available dataset consisting of English and Greek sentences with annotated semantic relations. DiscSense includes 720 sentences, with 12 possible relations and three categories of discourse markers. We also created evaluation benchmarks for identifying discourse markers and predicting relations.

Building upon the classical definition of the star product, we develop a generalized form of the Jordanian twist within the context of quantum groups. This generalized twist is found to be equivalent to a simple, reshaped Jordanian twist, demonstrating that the higher-order terms in the twist parameter do not contribute to the resulting algebra.

We enhance Brzozowski's defining regular expression operator to enable constructive proofs for checking if the regular expression R is contained within S. This enhanced operator performs a variety of tasks including multiplying regular expressions, taking complements, avoiding repetition in alternating expressions, and sharing variables between alternating expressions.

We provide a detailed derivation of the conserved current block OPE in three-dimensional CFT, utilizing an AdS$_3$ geodesic description, and subsequently convert it to the AdS$_2$ geodesic description.  Our calculation commences with the general, closed form of the AdS$_3$ block and performs the necessary transformation to obtain the AdS$_2$ version, which we then present in both exponential and momentum space.  We also outline the necessary ingredients for computing three-point functions involving conserved currents in CFT$_3$ using AdS$_3$ or AdS$_2$ geodesic descriptions.  Our derived AdS$_2$ block agrees with the existing result obtained through different methods.  By integrating the block with a specific CFT$_3$ three-point function, we verify that the resulting three-point function matches between AdS$_2$ and AdS$_3$ descriptions.  We further validate the consistency of our AdS$_2$ block by analyzing its symmetry properties and computing its dimension.  Finally, we outline the necessary steps for employing the AdS$_2$ block in computing four-point functions involving conserved currents in CFT$_3$.

Implementing advanced image processing techniques, we have developed a method to identify specific segments of a lobster-eye optics system based on the rotation of a cross-like image projected onto the system. By analyzing the azimuthal rotation angle of zero-thick cross-like images, we determine the boundaries of the system's segments. Our measurements show that for a 2mm thick lobster-eye optics system, segments 1 and 2 exhibit distinct properties, allowing us to distinguish them based on the image processing technique used. However, for thicker systems like the 5mm model, additional segmentation is required, which we achieve by analyzing the rotation angle of cross-like images with varying thickness.

This research examines the precision of halo mass predictions resulting from a cosmological hydrodynamic simulation, where a given region of interest is substituted with an external, physically consistent environment defined by the average properties of the region. A $512^3$ particle N-body simulation is used to test this approach, with a view to assessing its predictive capability concerning halo mass, which proves highly accurate as the model merely describes the behavior of dark matter under gravitational influence. With only minor modifications, the scenario is further explored where the external environment is defined by the average properties of a given halo, which in this case is a massive galaxy cluster. Here, the model's ability to predict halo mass through the halo's own properties is assessed, with an initial condition of moderate density perturbations used to simulate the scenario. With this setup, surprising results are obtained where the model's predictive capability concerning halo mass falls short, which raises intriguing questions concerning the role of wave function collapse in quantum cosmology, particularly with regard to the relationship between mass and the rate of halo formation/decay.

The local magnetic field's sensitivity for detection through atomic interferometry has been examined and a new record of 1.7 x 10^-15 Tesla m/s squared root Hz has been set. This achievement utilizes a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer with rubidium atoms, whose relative velocity needs to be precision-measured for magnetic field variation detection. The technique's sensitivity is comparable to, yet slightly lower than, local gravitational field detection sensitivity under identical conditions.

We perform a detailed analysis of how the spin-orbit coupling influences the placement of the Little-Parks (YSR) states on Cu(100) in the presence of adatoms or a paired adatom magnetization. Utilizing a theoretical framework that incorporates the nanoscale spin structure, we resolve the spin-dependent electron behavior by employing a tight-binding model combined with the Green's function approach. The results show that the spin-orbit effect causes a significant shift in the YSR state peaks, even when the adatom pair is distant from each other. Furthermore, we observe that the proximity effect significantly diminishes the YSR state presence on the surface, whereas the magnetic influence remains localized. The findings highlight the importance of considering the spin structure and spin-orbit coupling when examining the YSR states, particularly in scenarios involving adatom pairs or a close-packed atomic lattice like in the Cu(100) structure.

Deepening our understanding of convolutional neural network behavior
through ensemble methods has yielded significant gains in image
classification tasks. By harnessing the strengths of various CNN
architectures, ensemble classifiers have emerged as a powerful tool
for improving performance and robustness. In the process of doing
so, novel combinations of pre-existing networks have given birth
to several top-performing models, including the current leaders
EfficientNet and RegNet. In this paper, we initiate an in-depth
examination of the underlying reasons why ensemble classifiers
exhibit enhanced classification capabilities. Through a comprehensive
analysis of multiple ensemble models and various evaluation metrics,
we uncover a direct correlation between overall performance and
an index derived from layer growth patterns. Furthermore, we develop
a simple yet effective methodology for predicting the performance
of arbitrary ensemble models before actual implementation.

The structure functions for W and Z bosons in nucleons are examined using an effective field theory that incorporates universal corrections. This approach differs from the standard model but preserves key features, especially when analyzing hard scattering processes. Consistent with similar studies, it's found that the ratio of structure functions for protons and deuterons exhibits no significant effects from universal corrections. However, when comparing the structure functions for protons and neutrons, subtle influences become apparent, specifically in scenarios where two-body non-relativistic physics is significant. Latest measurements suggesting an ultraperipheral component in the ratio of structure functions for protons and deuterons require further investigation.

We extend Rosser's result, showing that inconsistent formal systems lack determinacy not just at a certain level but below it. This extended principle offers a more nuanced understanding of logical statements within formal systems.
The paper under review introduces a new concept of a fractional linear complement subsystem.

This paper explores how an initial condition can be reconstructed from pressure measurements in a fluid flow, given that the velocity field remains unknown. We solve an inverse problem involving a PDE, utilizing specific regularization techniques to ensure the problem's stability. The problem's stability is guaranteed by using observability inequalities, which involve additional regularization methods to account for the boundary measurements. Reconstructing the initial condition requires combining the regularization methods, as well as identifying suitable function spaces in which to operate.

We propose a minimalistic approach to explaining dark matter through a dark sector, which is completely isolated from the standard model due to a symmetry known as dark parity. This sector is incorporated into a standard model-based framework that includes an inert scalar representation, resulting in a minimal dark matter model. To avoid lepton flavor violation, we introduce a new heavy lepton doublet above specific mass thresholds. Through a process known as dark parity breaking, we generate dark sector asymmetry, which subsequently switches to the visible sector, allowing for the creation of dark matter in a form of a cold plasma. To calculate the vacuum stability and consistency of the dark parity symmetry, we employ the Coleman-Weinberg approach, Metadynamics, and the renormalization group equation. The paper's key findings include equations for (messenger) mass thresholds, vacuum stability bounds, and the RGE for the dark sector's dark doublet mass.
